questions.q: What is a PID, and which process always gets PID 1 on a modern Linux system?
options: A unique process ID; systemd always gets PID 1 since it's the first process the kernel starts at boot
A unique process ID; the kernel randomly assigns PID 1 to whichever process starts first
A memory address, unrelated to which process started first
PID 1 is always reserved for the root user's login shell
questions.explain: The kernel starts systemd first at boot, so it always receives PID 1 on a modern Linux distribution.

questions.q: What's the difference between SIGTERM (plain kill) and SIGKILL (kill -9)?
options: SIGTERM politely asks a process to clean up and exit; SIGKILL terminates it immediately with no chance to clean up
They are identical — both always force-kill a process instantly
SIGTERM only works on services, SIGKILL only works on ordinary processes
SIGKILL is deprecated and no longer does anything on modern Linux
questions.explain: SIGTERM is a request a well-behaved process can catch and clean up after; SIGKILL is unconditional and immediate, which is why it's a last resort.

questions.q: Why should you try a plain kill before kill -9 on a stuck process?
options: SIGTERM lets a well-behaved process close files and connections cleanly, while SIGKILL gives it no chance to clean up, risking corruption
kill -9 is actually slower to execute than a plain kill
There's no real difference, it's purely a matter of preference
Plain kill only works on processes owned by root
questions.explain: A database or server killed with SIGKILL mid-write can leave corrupted files behind; SIGTERM gives it a chance to finish and exit cleanly.

questions.q: Why did systemd replace older init systems like SysVinit on most Linux distributions?
options: It starts independent services in parallel, tracks dependencies explicitly, and uses one consistent unit file format instead of bespoke scripts
It was required by a new law governing open-source software
SysVinit was removed from the Linux kernel entirely
systemd only runs on cloud servers, not physical machines
questions.explain: SysVinit started services sequentially using inconsistent shell scripts; systemd's parallel startup and standard unit files were both faster and more consistent.

questions.q: What does systemctl enable sshd actually do, as opposed to systemctl start sshd?
options: enable makes the service start automatically on every future boot; start only starts it immediately, for the current session
enable and start do exactly the same thing
enable immediately stops the service, start immediately restarts it
enable only works for systemd services, start only works for SysVinit services
questions.explain: start/stop/restart act on the service right now; enable/disable control whether it survives a reboot.
